items.title: Mankato, Minnesota Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: J.C. Wise presented Owney with this round brass medal to wear as a tag while the dog was visiting Mankato, Minnesota. The date of the visit is indicated as June 17, 1895.

items.title: Express Saloon token, Cloverdale, California Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token, good for one drink or cigar from C. E. Mitchell’s “Express Saloon.” Mitchell emigrated from Germany in 1858, settling down in Cloverdale, California. His saloon may have been a popular stop for railway and railway mail workers working on board the San Francisco and Northern Pacific Railroad. This type of token is known as a trade check. These tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular disc with small uniform rim texture.

items.title: Bank of St. Helena Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 x 1 5/8 in. (1.59 x 4.13 cm)
items.description: This token was given to Owney in St. Helena, California during his travels on the Central Pacific Railroad. The token advertises a $1.00 reward for the return of the item it would have been attached to. Tokens such as these, commonly known as key tokens, were used to identify their owners in case of loss. There is no date to indicate when this was given to Owney. The key token’s text instructs that the item should be returned to the Bank of St. Helena in St. Helena, California.
items.shapeEvidence: Long horizontal oval body with rounded ends.

items.title: Stude's Coffee Parlor Houston Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: This is one of two tokens Owney received from Alphonse Stude’s Houston, Texas, bakery. Stude, a prominent Houston businessman and city booster, recognized the advertising potential of the traveling dog. Usually Owney’s arrival to a town was heralded in the local newspaper and the articles about his welcome often listed the tokens he was wearing. This token, which could be used in trade for a cup of coffee, is known as a trade check. These tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular disc; the small lower-edge hole is excluded.

items.title: Indian Head Penny Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 × 3/4 in. (1.91 × 1.91 cm)
items.description: This 1893 US coin, known as an “Indian head penny,” was one of several coins given to Owney during his travels. There is no record of when, or where, the dog received this token.
items.shapeEvidence: Round medallion body with a lightly serrated outer rim.

items.title: Travelers Preferred Accident Association Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token while in Chicago, the most active railway town in the United States. The donor was from the “Travelers Preferred Accident Association,” a well known insurance company of the time. There is no additional information indicating the name of the donor or the date Owney received this token. This style of identification token was often attatched to items, such as keys, that might be lost.
items.shapeEvidence: Wide horizontal oval with a smooth continuous outline.

items.title: Shea & Weaver Louisville, Kentucky Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)

There is no additional information to indicate when the token was given to the dog. Trade check tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular disc with fine evenly spaced rim serrations.

items.title: Saloon Token Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)

items.title: G&C railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)

items.shapeEvidence: Round disc with a continuous circular body outline.

items.title: Brunswick Token Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this trade check token for 5-cents off from “The Brunswick,” an establishment located at “15 W. Gay” street in an unidentified city. There is no additional information to indicate when or where this token was added to Owney’s collection. This token, is known as a trade check. These tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.
items.shapeEvidence: Round token body with small regular rim serrations.

items.title: George Washington Medal Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 × 1/8 in. (3.8 × 3.8 × 0.3 cm)
items.description: Owney received this advertising token from an unknown donor. The token celebrates President George Washington on one side, including an image and his birth and death dates, and aluminum, on the other. The U.S.’s first large aluminum refinery appeared in 1888, and the medal began to be used for tokens a few years later. The medal made its big splash with the American public at the Chicago World’s Fair in 1893. James Murdock, Jr. was already manufacturing tokens in brass, copper, and silver by the early 1890s and eagerly added aluminum to his business. This advertising token touts the metal on the back as “the new metal aluminum extracted from the common clay of the earth.” Murdock’s business was located in Cincinnati, Ohio.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular coin-like body with an evenly textured rim.

items.title: Thomas Metcalf Saloon Token Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this trade check token for 5-cents off of goods from Thomas Metcalf, a merchant of unknown goods or services. There is no additional information to indicate when or where the token was given to the dog. This token, is known as a trade check. These tokens were used much as coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.
items.shapeEvidence: Round disc with small uniform edge serrations.

items.title: Leland House Hotel Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3 1/4 × 3 1/4 in. (8.26 × 8.26 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel key token from the Leland House hotel in Winnipeg, Manitoba. The original number, 16, was scratched out and replaced with the number 51. The hotel was the city’s largest and most prominent hotel of the age. A few of Owney’s railway journeys took him into Canada, including one that took him aboard the Canadian Pacific railroad.
items.shapeEvidence: Many-ray sunburst contour surrounding a round center.

items.title: Nashville, Tennessee Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 2 3/16 × 1 3/4 × 1/16 in. (5.56 × 4.45 × 0.16 cm)
items.description: Many of Owney’s travels were celebrated in local newspapers. Newspaper reporters were second only to postal employees in their interest in the wandering canine. Owney received this token from the Nashville Banner, a newspaper that was published in Nashville, Tennessee from 1876-1998. The token notes that it was presented to the dog in April 1892.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad upper shoulders taper through curved sides to a bottom point.

items.title: Canadian Pacific Railway Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 3/8 x 1 7/8 in. (6.03 x 4.76 cm)
items.description: Owney occasionally traveled on Canadian railways, including the eastern portion of the Canadian Pacific Railroad. This baggage token, marked “Special P. 2847” was given to Owney during one of his trips on that railroad. The “Special” marking was used for travelers whose baggage would follow their journey off of the main railway onto another line. Railroad companies had agreements to return these specially marked tokens to the railroad of origin.
items.shapeEvidence: Straight-sided rectangular plate with broadly rounded bottom corners.

items.title: Hotel Occidental Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3 1/4 × 3 1/4 in. (8.26 × 8.26 cm)
items.description: The locations of some of the tokens Owney received on his journeys are impossible to track down. This flowery metal token offers few clues to its origin. “Occidental” was a popular name for hotels in the late nineteenth century--no other information on this token provides a clue as to where Owney received this strikingly-shaped hotel key token.
items.shapeEvidence: Sunburst body with many large pointed rays.

items.title: Leland House Hotel Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 5 x 2 3/4 in. (12.7 x 6.99 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel key check token from a hotel called the “Leland House.” There were at least three hotels in the U.S. with that name during Owney’s lifetime, and nothing on the token indicates which city was home to this particular hotel.
items.shapeEvidence: Four straight sides form a tall diamond.

items.title: Hotel Key Check Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 4 x 3 in. (10.16 x 7.62 cm)
items.description: The locations of some of the tokens Owney received on his journeys are impossible to track down. This diamond-shaped metal token is marked simply “E 33 H” and offers no clues to its origin. It is similar in markings to hotel key tokens Owney received along his journeys, but without additional information it is impossible to definitively identify it as such.
items.shapeEvidence: Four angular sides form a diamond-shaped body.

items.title: Railway Mail Service Washington, D.C. Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 x 1 3/4 in. (5.4 x 4.45 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token from James E. White’s office. White served as the General Superintendent of the Railway Mail Service from 1890 to 1907. The token, dated April 13, 1892, is a reminder of the admiration and respect Owney held in even the highest office of the nation’s Railway Mail Service.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad badge shoulders, concave sides and a tapered pointed lower end form a shield silhouette.

items.title: B. & P.T. Co. Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 3/4 × 1 1/2 × 1/16 in. (4.4 × 3.81 × 0.16 cm)
items.description: According to the information available on this token, Owney received it from a line or company known by the initials B&P, located in or near El Paso. The item, probably a baggage check token, does not provide enough information to indicate where or when it was given to the dog.
items.shapeEvidence: Tall rectangular plate with small rounded corners.

items.title: Manitoba Hotel Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token during one of his trips into Canada. The token was used in a grand hotel’s coat room. The Manitoba was a large seven-story, fashionably furnished hotel built in Winnipeg, the capital of Manitoba Province, Canada. The hotel, built about 1890 on Water Avenue, was destroyed less than a decade later in a fire in 1899. The hotel was a convenient stop for Owney, as it had been funded by the Northern Pacific and Manitoba Railway (N.P. & M.R.) and was located next to the N.P. & M.R. offices.
items.shapeEvidence: Round disc with a smooth overall circumference.

items.title: Lawrence, Massachusetts Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 x 3 in. (5.72 x 7.62 cm)
items.description: While visiting Lawrence, Massachusetts on June 13, 1894, Owney received a very personalized token. Those who gave the dog this token engraved a poem on it for all to see: “At Lawrence Mass. they took me in. And fed me well. It wasn’t thin. To the M. L. & B. north, they sent me then. And I hope to see them all again.” The MB&L was the Manchester, Lawrence & Boston Railway Post Office line.
items.shapeEvidence: A broad rectangular plate with nearly straight upper and side edges, rounded corners and minor bottom-edge notches.

items.title: New York Post Office Owney Tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 13/16 × 3 1/8 × 1/16 in. (4.6 × 7.94 × 0.16 cm)
items.description: Owney may have received this token from a letter carrier. The token is actually a cap badge style worn by U.S. letter carriers of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The badge is number 73 from the Brooklyn, New York, post office. There is no additional information to indicate the name of the person who gave this token to Owney, or when it was received. The city of Brooklyn was one Owney visited several times during his travels, and he received at least seven tokens during those visits.
items.shapeEvidence: Oval central badge has integral pointed ribbon-like extensions at both sides.

items.title: Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: There is not enough information on this token to indicate when or where it was given to Owney. It may be an Egyptian coin, and if so, would have been given to the dog during his around the world adventure in the fall of 1895.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular medallion body with small rim serrations.

items.title: Hotel Snoqualmie Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney may have received this token for room #137 of the Hotel Snoqualmie while visiting Seattle, Washington. A hotel of that name was located on Pike Street near 1st Avenue in Seattle in the early to mid 1890s. During his lifetime, Owney made a number of trips to the cities of Seattle and Tacoma, Washington, including his famous 1895 August trip, when he set out from Tacoma to travel with mailbags around the world.
items.shapeEvidence: Tall rectangular body with straight sides and rounded corners.

items.title: Chinook, Montana Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token on May 14, 1893. The donor inscribed his initials on the back side of the token, “B.E.N.” along with the town name Chinook, Montana, which is near the Canadian border. The token itself is from a railroad that was serviced by the Minnesota & Northwestern Railroad (“M.&N.W.R.R.”) as well as the St. Paul, Minneapolis, and Manitoba Railway Company (“StP.M&M.RY.”). The token would have been used as a receipt for checked baggage along one of the lines. As neither line appears to have passed through Chinook, it is impossible to say where Owney actually received this token.
items.shapeEvidence: A nearly square baggage-check plate with straight edges and rounded corners; the elongated slot is internal.

items.title: Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
items.description: The locations of some of the tokens Owney received on his journeys are impossible to track down. This circular metal token is marked simply with the numbers “50” and “3” and offers no clues to its origin.
items.shapeEvidence: Round main disc; the separate hanging ring is excluded.

items.title: R.N.I. & B. Railroad baggage claim check Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 3/8 in. (3.81 x 3.49 cm)
items.description: Owney probably received this token while riding on the Richmond, Nicholasville, Irving & Beattyville railroad in Kentucky. The token is a baggage check, which was given to passengers to locate their luggage that was stored in the baggage hold for the trip. The line, nicknamed the Riney B, operated from 1888 to 1902. The Riney B was named for the largest towns along its route through central Kentucky: Richmond, Irvine, Nicholasville, and Beattyville. The railroad’s carriage of mail and passengers was almost secondary to its use to bring lumber and coal across the state. The token was created by metal maker James Murdock of Cincinnati, Ohio. The back side of the token bears Murdock’s mark, noting that he was also at work as, or in, “seal presses, stamp cutting, engraver, and die sinker.”
items.shapeEvidence: Tall rectangular plaque with rounded corners.

items.title: Boston & Portland P.S. Packet Company Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 1 3/4 in. (4.13 x 4.45 cm)
items.description: Not all of Owney’s mail-related travels were on trains. Owney received this baggage check token from a sidewheel paddle steamboat. The Steamer Tremont, operated by the Portland Steam Packet Company, carried passengers and mail between Portland, Maine and Boston, Massachusetts. This boat was known as a nightboat, traveling between the two cities overnight. The baggage token, #13, would have been used to check a piece of passenger luggage during the trip. This baggage check was made by John Robbins, who began crafting such tokens in the early 1840s in Boston, Massachusetts.
items.shapeEvidence: Bell-like body widens below sloping shoulders and ends in two rounded lower lobes.

items.title: Kampeska House Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 13/16 x 1 3/4 in. (4.6 x 4.45 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel room check key token for room #40 from the Kampeska House hotel in Watertown, South Dakota. During the years that Owney could have visited the hotel, it was run by Cincinatus C. Wiley, a Civil War veteran originally from Massachusetts. Owney may have arrived in Watertown on one of a number of railway lines, including the Minneapolis & St. Paul; the Northwestern; or the Burlington & Cedar Rapids.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad upper shoulders narrow down to a central bottom point.

items.title: Atlanta, Georgia Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 x 1 1/2 in. (3.49 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this brass shield-shaped tag on a visit to Atlanta, Georgia. The tag is dated April 8, 1892. The tag includes the initials RMS, which stands for Railway Mail Service. There is no information available to indicate who presented the tag to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad angular shoulders and indented sides taper into a central bottom point; the upper slot is internal.

items.title: Newberry's Bus Line Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
items.description: Owney may have received this transportation token (“good for 1 ride”) from the “Newberry’s Bus line” of Ft. Dodge, Iowa. That bus line provided tokens for riders to and from the town’s railway station. A number of railway lines passed through Ft. Dodge, including the Illinois Central, the Chicago, Rock Island, and Pacific, and the Mason City and Fort Dodge lines.
items.shapeEvidence: Round disc with a continuous circular perimeter.

items.title: Atlantic & Pacific Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 1/2 in. (3.18 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this baggage check token while aboard an Atlantic & Pacific Railroad mail car. The railway’s title was a bit of a misnomer. The railroad was operated in two separate segments, neither of which touched on the Atlantic coast. One segment ran between St. Louis, Missouri to Tulsa, Oklahoma. The second segment ran from Albuquerque, New Mexico into California. The local marking indicates that the passenger and baggage would have traveled only on this line, not onto a connecting one. This baggage check token was created by William W. Wilcox, a Chicago-based manufacturer.
items.shapeEvidence: Squarish rectangular plate with straight sides and rounded corners.

items.title: Oregon and California Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (4.45 x 3.49 cm)
items.description: Owney would have received this baggage check token while on the Oregon and California Railroad. The O&C began in Oregon and operated from 1869-1972, although the line did not cross the California border until 1887, a year before Owney began his travels. This baggage check token was created by William W. Wilcox, a Chicago-based manufacturer.
items.shapeEvidence: Rectangular plaque with straight side edges and small stepped end corners.

items.title: Yellowstone Hotel Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney’s travels may have taken him to Yellowstone National Park, but as far as is known by his tokens, this may be as close as he got to that famous area. He probably received this hotel key token while visiting the Yellowstone Hotel in Glendive, Montana. The town is located near the border of Montana and North Dakota. The town was a stop along the Northern Pacific Railroad during Owney’s lifetime. The token itself was manufactured by “NW Stamp Works,” a northwest company that also manufactured police badges, rubber stamps for city offices, date stamps, and dog license tokens.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular disc body despite slight wear along the rim.

items.title: O'Connor's Hotel Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 3/4 x 2 1/4 in. (6.99 x 5.72 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel key check token while visiting O’Connor’s Hotel in Winnipeg, Canada. Owney made at least one trip to Winnipeg during his lifetime, in the summer of 1895, just a month before he started off on his journey around the world.
items.shapeEvidence: Straight angular edges form a six-point star; hanging eyelet excluded.

items.title: Naugatuck Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 3/4 in. (3.81 x 4.45 cm)
items.description: Owney received this baggage check token from someone along the Naugatuck Railroad. The Naugatuck operated in Connecticut as a connecting line from the New York & New Haven RR. It merged with that company in 1906. This baggage check was made by John Robbins, who began crafting such tokens in the early 1840s in Boston, Massachusetts.
items.shapeEvidence: Ornamental plaque has four broad end lobes and deeply indented side shoulders.

items.title: Vancouver Hotel Owney tag
places: British Columbia & Vancouver Island (British colony; Canadian pr
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 13/16 x 1 1/2 in. (4.6 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel baggage check token while visiting the Vancouver Hotel in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. The hotel operated from 1887-1916. Owney is known to have made at least a half dozen trips across the border into Canada during his lifetime. The date Owney received this token is undetermined, but it is known that visited the area in 1895. Another famous world traveler, Mark Twain, stayed at the same hotel in mid August 1895 while on a lecture tour. There is no evidence the two ever crossed paths, but the hotel was evidently the choice for world travelers, human and canine alike.
items.shapeEvidence: Tall straight-sided rectangle with rounded corners.

items.title: Columbia House Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 13/16 x 1 1/2 in. (4.6 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel key check token from a hotel known as “Columbia House.” Even though the proprietor’s name, W. Bohn, is known, there is not yet any information on where or when the dog received this trinket.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad upper shoulders taper through curved sides to a lower point.

items.title: Guichon Hotel Owney tag
places: British Columbia & Vancouver Island (British colony; Canadian pr
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 4 13/16 x 3 1/2 in. (12.22 x 8.89 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel key check token while on a trip into Canada. The token would have been used to identify the key to room #32 at the Guichon Hotel in North Westminster, British Columbia, now a suburb of Vancouver, British Columbia. The dog probably arrived in town along the Canadian Pacific Railway in the early 1890s.
items.shapeEvidence: Four straight sides form a tall diamond.

items.title: Owney tag marked R.H.
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: This brass octagonal tag is marked with the initials R.H. and the number "2." There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, who presented it, or where.
items.shapeEvidence: Eight straight edges form an octagonal body.

items.title: Station G Brooklyn, New York Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1/8 x 2 1/4 in. (0.32 x 5.72 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token while visiting Brooklyn, New York in early April 1894. The token is dated “Apr. 12 -94” on the back and the front indicates Owney’s visit was to the Station G Brooklyn post office. According to the Brooklyn Daily Eagle Almanac from 1891, Station G served a district from “the East River and Newtown Creek along creek to Meeker Avenue, to Richardson Street, to Union Avenue, to North 14th, to East River.” The Brooklyn Daily Eagle newspaper from April 9, 1894 recorded Owney’s arrival in the area. In the story with a playful headline, “Inspector Owney Here,” the paper refers to the dog as “a visitor of national reputation,” and recorded his visit to the main Brooklyn post office, where he was welcomed by Postmaster Andrew T. Sullivan.
items.shapeEvidence: A long narrow plate with parallel straight upper and lower edges and slightly chamfered short ends.

items.title: Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 2 1/8 in. (2.54 x 5.4 cm)
items.description: There is no definitive information that indicates where or when Owney received this token. The names G. Grafton and H. McGowan do not appear in the same post office together in any of the US registers of the Post Office Department during the 1890s.
items.shapeEvidence: Long eight-sided plaque with four clear diagonal corner cuts.

items.title: South Dakota Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token while traveling in South Dakota. The item is an advertisement for Black Hills tin. During the early 1890s, the area experienced a boom in Black Hills tin, but by 1893 the boom had gone bust. The token, made from Black Hills tin, is engraved with the words “In the spirit of love and justice the people rule.” It is not known who gave the token to Owney, or where in South Dakota he may have received it.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular medal body with small regular rim serrations.

items.title: Holly Springs Hotel Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 7/8 x 1 3/4 in. (4.76 x 4.45 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel key check token from the Holly Springs Hotel in Holly Springs, Mississippi. The token, which would have been used for room key #22, indicates that the hotel was possibly owned by the Illinois Central railroad. That railroad, along with the Kansas, Memphis, and Birmingham, passed through the town of Holly Springs. The hotel was located near at the train tracks, and would have been used by traveling railway mail clerks as well as regular railway employees.
items.shapeEvidence: Angular plaque has four pronounced diagonal corner cuts and short flat ends.

items.title: Banner Division Cincinnati, Ohio Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token while visiting Cincinnati, Ohio on April 11, 1892. There is no additional information to identify the “Banner Division 5th” identified on the front portion of the token. The back has an engraver’s mark from James Murdock Jr., a Cincinnati engraver and metals manufacturer.
items.shapeEvidence: The brass token is a round disc, with a large hole near the top edge.

items.title: H. J. Thyes Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 × 1 3/8 in. (3.49 × 3.49 cm)
items.description: Owney received this trade check token from Herman J. Thyes, who worked as a liquor salesman in Reno, Nevada in the 1890s. Thyes produced a series of such tokens during his business career. Trade checks such as these were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases. This token offered the owner “one drink or cigar” on one side, with a list of products for sale on the other. At some point in his career Thyes was the proprietor of The Crystal saloon on 2nd Street in Reno.
items.shapeEvidence: Round disc with a fine uniformly serrated rim.

items.title: Hotel Claremont Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 × 1 5/8 in. (4.13 × 4.13 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel key check token while visiting the Hotel Claremont in Claremont, New Hampshire. There is no additional information available on when Owney received the token. The three-story hotel was designed by William Ralph Emerson, a cousin of the famous writer, Ralph Waldo Emerson. The hotel was located on the northern side of Tremont Square and was built in 1892.
items.shapeEvidence: Round disc; large internal hanging hole excluded.

items.title: US Mail Service Owney tag

items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 3 in. (3.81 x 7.62 cm)
items.description: Owney probably received this token from a representative of Harrison’s manufacturing business. A former postal employee, Harrison partnered with William P. Towne, forming the Charles Harrison & Company manufacturers of brass and plumbers’ supplies in Fond du Lac, Wisconsin. In 1890, the company ran into financial difficulties. Harrison managed to continue producing products, including the “mail distributing rack” that is advertised on this token. He patented the rack on April 8, 1879, patent #214,036. Harrison’s “system of mail-car fixtures and furniture of portable drop-tables and bag racks” had the welfare of the Railway Mail Service clerks in mind. It was designed to “more fully utilize the space, admit light from the windows, secure better ventilation, economize time, facilitate work, lessen the number and individual labor of clerks.” Harrison made the mail racks his life’s work. In the 1900 census, at age 77, Harrison listed his occupation as “Manufactures Postal Racks.”

items.title: Tacoma, Washington Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
items.description:
Among Owney’s more unusual tokens is this one given to him from the Tacoma [Washington] Poultry Association. The association held a show between December 31, 1895 and January 4, 1896, and quite possibly Owney was visiting the city at that time. Given Owney’s demonstrated fondness for chasing chickens, it is hard to imagine he would have behaved himself at a poultry show. Just two years earlier Owney had rewarded a California clerk’s hospitality by chasing the family’s chickens. By the time the clerk responded to the wild cackling and squawking in his yard, Owney was found with the “finest and largest fowl of the yard” in his mouth.

Reference:

Los Angeles Times, “Owney’s ‘Fowl’ Crime,” April 30, 1893, p. 7.

items.description: This metal shield-shaped tag was given to Owney on his visit to Detroit, Michigan, on November 11, 1893. Just as Owney’s presence in a city was an opportunity to interest the local press in an unusual story, Owney was a walking billboard for civic organizations and store owners. Owney’s Detroit tag advertised the city as the “Beautiful City of the Straits” to those who met the dog after his visit there.
items.shapeEvidence: Angular upper shoulders, concave side edges and a tapered central bottom point form a shield body.

items.title: US Post Office Department Washington, D.C. Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 × 2 1/8 in. (5.4 × 5.4 cm)
items.description:
Owney received this token from the postal workers whose jobs were to repair the thousands of mailbags and mail locks that were damaged during service. Given the purported love of Owney for the smell of mailbags, this shop would have been a necessary stop. The token notes that it was presented to Owney on April 13, 1892. At that time, the Washington, DC repair shop was the center of Department’s bag and lock repair work. Superintendent Franklin B. Kirkbridge managed a shop of 230 workers (120 men; 110 women) located at 479 and 481 C Street, NW. The five-story tall building held workers who repaired and returned into service 200,000 mailbags each month.

Of the workers who were employed at the repair shop, women were employed for the most part in piece work on the jute canvas sacks. They sewed the bags, repaired and restrung them as needed at the rate of 3 1/2 cents per bag. They were expected to finish 38 bags each day. The male workers were paid by the month, $75 a month for leather and canvas workers; $50 a month for the laborers who received, shook out, handled, packed, and reshipped the bags after they had been repaired.
items.shapeEvidence: The repair-shop token has a round outer perimeter, independent of its engraved lettering.

The token notes the special relationship between the dog and the nation’s Railway Mail Service employees, noting that he was a “faithful friend.” There is no notation on the token indicating when it was presented to the traveler. Owney visited New York City on a regular basis during his lifetime, and he could have received it almost anytime during his lifetime.

The back of the token is dated 1892. Anderson, a Scottish immigrant, worked as a clerk for several years before transferring over to Omaha’s Free City Delivery service as a letter carrier. items.title: Charlestown, Massachusetts Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 × 2 1/8 in. (5.4 × 5.4 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag from a visit to Charlestown, Massachusetts. The round brass tag notes that Owney “called on” Dan Kelly’s grocery store on June 22, 1894.
items.shapeEvidence: A circular disc with many small uniform serrations around its circumference; the fine teeth retain its dominant round body.

items.title: Brooklyn, New York Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 2 1/2 in. (1.91 x 6.35 cm)
items.description: On occasion, people presented Owney with tags that dogs would naturally have, such as this one from Brooklyn, New York. It is a dog license tag, number 5758. The date, 1891, indicates it may be one of the earliest tags in the collection. There is no indication whether it was presented to Owney then or whether the tag was left over from an earlier year.
items.shapeEvidence: Long ornamental label has scalloped edges and lobed ends.

items.title: Jackson, Mississippi Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: The design of this oval-shaped, metal tag is relatively common among the Owney tags. This one is marked "Wilson Parker, I.C.L. Counter, Jackson, Miss." There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Wide horizontal oval with continuous curved ends.

items.title: Buffalo, New York Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
items.description: Postal workers at the Buffalo, New York, post office presented this round brass tag to Owney on May 24, 1893. It is one of the earliest tags in Owney’s collection. At first, Owney did not travel far from home, including this May trip.
items.shapeEvidence: The postal tag is a round disc with a small hole at its upper edge.

items.title: Boston, Providence and NY Night Express Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 3/4 x 2 in. (6.99 x 5.08 cm)
items.description: W.J. Tilley of the Boston, Providence, and New York City night mail train welcomed Owney to the train car with this tag, which is dated April 27, 1892.
items.shapeEvidence: A badge with flared shoulders, an inward-curving waist, a broad lower bowl and a central bottom point.

items.title: Winona, Minnesota Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: This brass, triangular-shaped key was presented to Owney at Winona, Minnesota. The tag carries the date June 16, 1895, on the back.
items.shapeEvidence: Two long sloping sides rise to a top apex above a broad flat base; small clipped lower corners do not change the dominant triangular body.

items.title: Lawrence, Massachusetts Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 2 in. (2.54 x 5.08 cm)
items.description: While visiting Lawrence, Massachusetts, Owney received this brass oval tag from George H. Leck’s photography studio. The tag includes the phrase “I had my Photo taken there.” If Owney did have a photograph taken at Leck’s studio, there is no known record of it.
items.shapeEvidence: Elongated horizontal oval body with a smooth outer outline.

items.title: Haverhill, Massachusetts Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag from a creative person in Haverhill, Massachusetts. The specially made token is inscribed with a poem, “This tag will tell you all the news; Owney has visited the city of shoes” and is dated June 16, 1894. There is no information on who gave this tag to the dog. This is one of several promotional tags given to Owney, treating the dog as something of a traveling advertisement.
items.shapeEvidence: Many large pointed and rounded rays form a sunburst silhouette; the outer edge is deeply lobed.

items.title: Nashville, Tennessee Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 1 1/2 in. (2.54 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: From time to time, Owney received tokens for goods on his journeys. This square brass token was redeemable for one quart of milk. It is undetermined whether the stamped letters "R.C.C." refer to a business. On the reverse side of the metal piece, someone etched: "Nashville, Tenn / Tom Glascock." According to census records from the time of Owney's travels, William J. Glascock, father of Thomas M. Glascock born 1874 in Tennessee, worked for railway mail and the family were living Tennessee around 1891 according to a voter registration list. (They were also listed in the 1880 Census in Fulton County, Georgia, where William Glascock worked for railway mail). There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney, but it is conceivable that someone carved young Tom's name into the metal piece, perhaps when William, Tom, and other family members of the Glascock family may have met Owney while William worked with the railway mail.
items.shapeEvidence: Squarish rectangular plate with rounded corners.

items.title: Louisville, Kentucky Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 1 in. (2.54 x 2.54 cm)
items.description: This octagon-shaped metal tag has markings on both sides. The front identifies it as having come from the Commonwealth Life Insurance Company of Louisville, Kentucky. The back proclaims the company’s motto, “United We Stand, Divided We Fall, A Square Deal for Every Policy Holder” with an image of two men shaking hands. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Ornamental squarish body has large inward-curved corner cutouts and uneven lower detailing.

items.title: Louisville, Kentucky Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: This token from a Louisville, Kentucky, store is marked “good for 5 cents trade or cash” at D.C. Brenner & Company. The company advertises its wears as including rubber stamps, stencils, seas, pool mining, and hotel checks. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Flower-like contour has several broad rounded lobes.

items.title: Herber W. Hull Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 in. (3.18 x 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag from Heber W. Hull of Plymouth, New Hampshire. Hull was a railroad employee and not associated with the Post Office Department. This tag notes Hull’s employer at the time, the Concord & Montreal Railroad. By 1905 Hull was working as a conductor for the C&M Railroad’s owner, the Boston & Maine Railroad. In addition to working for the railroads, Hull was a Mason. The circular symbol with the initials KSHTWSST notes that Hull was a Royal Arch Mason and Master Mason in his local lodge.
items.shapeEvidence: Main plate is a straight-sided trapezoid, wider at the top; hanging eyelet excluded.

items.title: Cincinnati, Ohio Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this pedal-shaped token from the Stag in Cincinnati. There is no additional information indicating when Owney received this tag. The Stag was a hotel as well as a saloon. The Stag saloon was owned by Tony Honing and Edwin W. Baylis. The hotel was advertised as “for gentlemen only” and as a “handy hotel popular with country merchants and commercial travelers” and was managed by Walter H. Maxwell.
items.shapeEvidence: Large rounded lobes form a flower-like outer contour.

items.title: J.F.C. Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
items.description: There is little information to indicate when or where Owney received this tag. It seems to have been given to him by an individual with the initials J.F.C. of Princeton, Indiana. The tag is marked on both sides with the notation K of H, or Knights of Honor, a lodge founded in 1873.
items.shapeEvidence: Round disc with a smooth continuous circumference.

items.title: Hornellsville, New York Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/8 x 1 3/8 in. (3.49 x 3.49 cm)
items.description: Owney received this decorated tag from Mason L. Wafer of Hornellsville, New York. There is no information indicating when Owney received the tag. Wafer was a business owner according to the 1891 Steuben County directory, but his business is not listed. If the illustration is any indication, it may well have been related to roller skating. Owney received two tags from this city’s businessmen. The other came from Fred D. Lockwood, a clerk in his father’s shoemaking business. Hornellsville was on at least two railway lines that Owney traveled, the New York & Erie and the Buffalo and New York City lines.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad angular upper shoulders taper through curved sides to a central bottom point.

items.title: Hotel Fife Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
items.description:
Owney received this hotel check key tag from the Hotel Fife in Tacoma, Washington. The five-story hotel, built in 1888, was located on the northwest corner of 9th and Pacific and was torn down in 1925. William H. Fife, the hotel’s owner, was born in Ontario, Canada. He was an important figure in the early days of Tacoma, building the first general store and acting as the city’s first postmaster (1874-1882) and became one of the city’s most prosperous citizens.

The tag itself was produced by the Talcott Brothers, who owned a jewelry business in Olympia, Washington, as is noted at the top portion of the tag. Lucius Ford Talcot and his son, Charles established the first business. Charles’ brothers George and Lucius Grant Talcott continued the work as the Talcott Brothers. The business thrived and grew, with the store selling more than just jewelry (bicycles and sewing machines, among other items). In 1889 the trio were asked to design the Washington state seal.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad angled shoulders narrow through curved side edges to a rounded lower point.

items.title: St. Paul & A. Lea Railway Post Office Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification token from an individual whose name appears to be Frank R. Hedrick of Chaska, Minnesota. The official Post Office Department registers of the time do not list any postal or railway mail service workers by that name during Owney’s travels. There is no additional information from the tag to indicate Hedrick’s connection to the Department.
items.shapeEvidence: Wide horizontal oval body with continuous rounded ends.

items.title: Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: There is no information associated with this tag to indicate when or where Owney received it, nor from whom. The only markings on the tags are the letter G, A, and F.
items.shapeEvidence: Round disk with a continuous circular rim.

items.title: J.P. Palmer Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification tag from J.P. Palmer of New York City, New York. There is no information on the tag to indicate when it was given to the dog, nor Palmer’s profession. The official registers of the Post Office Department for the 1890s do not list a J.P. Palmer in any New York postal facility.
items.shapeEvidence: Long horizontal body with smoothly rounded ends.

items.title: Knights of the Grip Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 2 1/2 in. (5.08 x 6.35 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag from a Michigan state association known as the “Knights of the Grip.” The group, an organization of traveling salesmen, was well known to railway employees, including postal clerks. The suitcase-shaped tag was the symbol of the group. Michigan’s “Knights of the Grip” allowed membership from anyone who “has been employed for the term of a year or more as a traveling man, and not over 50 years of age. In good health, not afflicted with any chronic disease, and not addicted to the use of intoxicating liquors as a beverage, residing or traveling in the State of Michigan.” Aside from the requirements that a member be a traveling “man” the traveling railway mail dog may well have been seen as a fellow knight by the salesmen.
items.shapeEvidence: Suitcase body has long straight opposite edges and squared corners.

items.title: Central Fire Station Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/4 in. (3.81 x 3.18 cm)
items.description: Owney received a handful of tags from firemen and fire stations around the country, including this tag representing Lowell, Massachusetts’s Central Fire Station. There is no information on when Owney received the tag. A number of railway lines passed through Lowell, including the Boston & Main and the Old Colony Railroad. The back of the tag notes that C.O.A. Grover, a Lowell steel letter cutter, created the tag.
items.shapeEvidence: Tall straight-sided plate with a flat base and small top shoulders.

items.title: Boston & Albany Railway Post Office Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
items.description: There is no information on when Owney received this tag, but it came from his friends in the Railway Mail Service. The tag notes that it was given by clerks of the Boston & Albany railway line, specifically those working in the Railway Post Office trains #5 and #12. The phrase “Always welcome on the no longer gilt edge” may be a reference to the usually reliably profitable Boston & Albany enduring a bad year.
items.shapeEvidence: Faceted perimeter has several distinct straight sides and angular corners.

items.title: Howard Young Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 x 1 1/4 in. (2.54 x 3.18 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification tag from Howard Young of St. Paul, Minnesota. Young worked as a brakeman for the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis, & Omaha railway. The tag is also inscribed “F.L.T.,” or Friendship, Love and Truth, a signifier of the fraternal organization known as the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. There is no information on the tag to indicate when Owney may have received it.
items.shapeEvidence: Pronounced ornamental scallops run around the perimeter.

items.title: Pontiac, Illinois Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 in. (1.91 x 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this trade check tag from Silas A. Rathbun, a Pontiac, Illinois businessman and active member of the state’s Democratic Party. Trade checks such as these were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases. This token offered the owner 25-cents off of a purchase of furniture in Rathbun’s Dry Goods store (which he later developed into a Department Store). Rathbun also served as the city’s mayor for a number of years (1889-1901, 1903-1905, and 1911-1913). There is no additional information on when this tag was given to Owney, but Rathbun’s first term as mayor overlapped the years of Owney’s travels. Thus, in the town of Pontiac, Illinois, Owney was greeted by the town mayor.
items.shapeEvidence: Four straight sides form a nearly square plate with rounded corners.

items.title: Postmaster William W. Johnson Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 in. (3.18 x 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag from William W. Johnson who served as Baltimore’s postmaster from 1890-1894. The shield-shaped tag includes a recognizable piece of the Baltimore landscape, the Washington Monument in Mt. Vernon square.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad shoulders narrow into a pointed lower tip.

items.title: F.D. Lockwood Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/4 in. (3.81 x 3.18 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag from Fred D. Lockwood of Hornellsville, New York. The tag is one of two Owney received from businessmen in that city. The other was from Mason L. Wafer, whose business may have been related to the roller skating industry. Lockwood was a clerk in his father’s shoemaking business. Hornellsville was on at least two railway lines that Owney traveled, the New York & Erie and the Buffalo and New York City lines.
items.shapeEvidence: Wide upper body tapers into a central bottom point.

items.title: George A. Reinville Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification tag from George A. Reinville, who is listed in the Manchester, New Hampshire city directories as first a clerk at an unidentified business on Merrimack Street, then a janitor at Union Depot. The tag notes that Mr. Reinville was a member of the Ancient Order of Foresters, a fraternal society rooted in England. The back of the tag is engraved with “Bakersville N.H.” and the initials “K.S. F.,” which may stand for the Knights of St. Francis.
items.shapeEvidence: Elongated horizontal oval with a smoothly curved rim.

items.title: Portland, Maine Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: The design of this oval-shaped, metal tag is relatively common among the Owney tags. The staff or proprietors at Lane & Collins, photographers at the Portland, Maine, railway station gave this tag to Owney. The tag indicates that Owney visited the station and studio on April 14, 1896.
items.shapeEvidence: An elongated oval plate with smoothly rounded ends and a hole near the left edge.

items.title: Seattle, Washington Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hand engraved tag during a visit to Seattle, Washington, on July 17, 1895. Owney made a number of trips to the Seattle / Tacoma area, including August 1895, when he started out on his around the world tour. There is no information to indicate who presented this tag to the dog.
items.shapeEvidence: A round dark medal with a continuous circular rim and a small internal top hole.

items.title: E.D. Simpson Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney was given this identification tag by E.D. Simpson of Running Water, South Dakota. The tag is dated 1893. There is no one by that name who worked for the Post Office Department during Owney’s lifetime, and no additional information that points to Mr. Simpson’s profession. The city of Running Water was served by the Chicago & Milwaukee Railway line.
items.shapeEvidence: Long oval body with rounded ends.

items.title: Kansas City, Missouri Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (1.91 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: From time to time Owney received practical gifts for his collar--dog tags. This one, from Kansas City, Missouri, is dated 1893 and shows that someone has covered Owney’s dog tax, permitting the pooch to wander the city without fear of arrest. There is no additional information to indicate who gave this tag to Owney. Kansas City was a railway hub, served by dozens of lines. Owney undoubtedly spent a great deal of time traveling through or wandering in the city.
items.shapeEvidence: Short horizontal plate has straight sides and rounded corners.

items.title: Railway Mail Service Superintendent Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 × 1 3/4 in. (4.45 × 4.45 cm)
items.description: Owney’s best friends among postal employees were the railway mail clerks who rode with him on trains. While in Boston, Massachusetts, Owney often spent time visiting not only the general city post office, but also the Railway Mail Service offices. At the time of this visit, the Division Superintendent of the RMS for Boston was Edward J. Ryan, who had started his career as a railway mail service clerk in 1868, riding the Boston and Albany Railway Post Office for $1,400 a year. The pride of the Railway Mail Service workers is evident in their boast of being “First in Everything” on this tag.
items.shapeEvidence: Deep rounded notches and broad gear-like teeth repeatedly interrupt the outer perimeter.

items.title: Council Bluffs, Iowa Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/4 in. (3.81 x 3.18 cm)
items.description: From time to time Owney received practical gifts for his collar – dog tags. This one, Council Bluffs, Iowa shows that someone has covered Owney’s dog tax in 1893, permitting the pooch to wander the city without fear of arrest. There is no additional information to indicate who gave this tag to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad lobed shoulders narrow toward a pointed lower end.

items.title: Washington DC City Post Office Owney tag
items.description: Owney received this tag from the Washington, DC city post office on April 13, 1892. The badge was given to the dog by the Registry (or Registered Mail) Division of the local post office. The badge-shaped token was created by William F. Lutz of 626 G Street, NW, a Prussian-born engraver.
items.shapeEvidence: Angular shoulders and curved inward sides broaden lower down before tapering to a central bottom point.

items.title: George W. Cooley Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token from George W. Cooley, a Railway clerk who worked on the Aberdeen and Sioux City Railway line. Cooley, born in Maryland, was appointed as a mail clerk in South Dakota and was making $1,000 a year as of 1895. The tag includes the date March 19, 1894. The tag was created by Oscar J. Hoberg, a local watchmaker. Hoberg worked for James G. Thompson & Sons in Sioux City, Iowa during the time Owney was traveling. By 1900, Hoberg was able to open his own watch repair shop with George Thorpe, “Thorpe & Hoberg.”
items.shapeEvidence: A round plate with a circular outer edge and a small internal top hole.

items.title: Hawthorne, Nevada Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: The back side of the token is an advertisement for the Brunswick-Balke-Collender Company. Originally a billiard equipment company, Brunswick-Balke-Collender produced phonograph cases for record players.
items.shapeEvidence: Main disk has a circular outer rim.

items.title: San Francisco, California Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
items.description: Owney received this round token while visiting San Francisco, California on April 12, 1893. The token was designed to resemble a cancellation marking, with the date “Apr 12” and time “3am” noted, as well as a “Rec’d” or received marking, noting undoubtedly the dog’s arrival. Owney was in San Francisco on his way south. On April 21, 1893, he was honored at a dog show in Los Angeles.
items.shapeEvidence: A round coin-like disc with a continuous circular border; the hole near the rim is internal.

items.title: Teegarden Hotel Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 1/2 in. (5.08 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: While visiting LaPorte, Indiana, on the Northern Indiana and South Michigan Railroad, Owney received this tag from the staff or proprietor of the Teegarden Hotel. The hotel had originally been built for Dr. Abram Teegarden when the railroad first reached LaPorte in 1852. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Tall plate retains straight opposite sides despite small stepped corners.

items.title: Hotel Fife Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: The most famous of Owney’s travels was his trip around the world in the late summer and fall of 1895. That trip began and ended in Tacoma, Washington, and it may have been during one of those times that he received this hotel key tag from that city’s Fife hotel. The hotel was built by William H. Fife, a businessman who had also served for eight years as the postmaster of the city of Tacoma.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad upper shoulders and curved sides taper to a bottom point.

items.title: New Jordan House Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: W. F. Jordan, the proprietor of the New Jordan House, presented this tag to Owney in honor of his visit to Brookings, South Dakota. There is no available information to indicate the date that this tag was presented to Owney. The tag was originally manufactured by W. W. Wilcox of Chicago, which was a major manufacturer of railroad baggage tags and similar metal items in the late nineteenth century. The Wilcox company produced at least two other Owney tags: 0.052985.173 and 0.052985.24.
items.shapeEvidence: Straight-sided tall plate has modest scalloped corner variations.

items.title: The Baldwin Hotel Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
items.description: This tag was given to Owney on his visit to one of San Francisco’s most prestigious hotels, The Baldwin, which was on the corner of Powell and Market streets until it was destroyed in a fire in 1898. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Main body is a near-circular disk.

items.title: Columbus, Hocking Valley & Toledo Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this metal tag when he rode train car #1583 of the Columbus, Hocking Valley and Toledo Railway Company line. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Four straight sides with gently rounded corners.

items.title: Pennsylvania and Erie Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 3/8 in. (3.81 x 3.49 cm)
items.description: This small metal tag was presented to Owney when he rode on the Pennsylvania and Erie Railroad, car number 7116. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Tall rectangular plate has long parallel sides and rounded corners.

items.title: Brooklyn, Bath and West End Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
items.description: Owney obtained this round metal tag while riding in New York City. He rode the Brooklyn, Bath and West End Railroad, which had been organized in 1885 out of the Brooklyn, Bath and Coney Island Railroad. There is no information on when he rode in this car, but it was probably before the line was electrified with trolley wire in 1893. At that time, the BB & WE merged with the Atlantic Avenue Railroad.
items.shapeEvidence: Round disk with an evenly curved outer boundary.

items.title: Chesapeake and Ohio Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/4 in. (3.81 x 3.18 cm)
items.description: This shield-shaped metal baggage tag was given to Owney by someone who worked along the Chesapeake and Ohio Railroad. The back of the tag indicates the agreement offered to the holder--“in consideration of free carriage of baggage, its value is agreed to be limited to one hundred dollars.” There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Flat upper shoulders lead into a strongly rounded tapering base.

items.title: Philadelphia, Wilmington, and Baltimore Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag when he rode a mail car on the Philadelphia, Wilmington, and Baltimore Railroad, train car #6829. The tag also includes a marking indicating the train traveled from northeast Maryland. There is no available information to indicate the date Owney received this tag.
items.shapeEvidence: Main body is circular around the slot.

items.title: Eastern Seaboard Trip Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 in. (4.45 cm)
items.description: This tag marks Owney’s travels on a series of small railway lines between Jersey City, New Jersey, to Jacksonville, Florida. Among the lines Owney traveled were the Pennsylvania and the Richmond, Fredericksburg and Potomac Railroad. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Tall plate has parallel sides, a flat base and rounded corners.

items.title: Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 x 1 1/2 in. (3.18 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag when he road on the Burlington and St. Louis portion of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad on June 22, 1895.
items.shapeEvidence: The baggage badge has broad angular upper shoulders, inward-curving side edges and a central lower point.

items.title: Manitoba Hall Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
items.description: While traveling in Canada, Owney visited Winnipeg, the capitol of the Canadian province Manitoba, north of Minnesota and North Dakota. Nothing on the tag indicates how Owney traveled to Winnipeg. He might have gone on the Duluth and Winnipeg railroad. This tag marks Owney's appearance at Manitoba Hall, a large, two-story building on Portage Avenue that was, in the 1890s, the largest building in the city. There is no available information to indicate either the nature of the event held at the hall during his visit or when he received this tag.
items.shapeEvidence: Deep rounded rays make a sunburst outline.

items.title: San Francisco, California Owney tag
items.description: J. Coyne of San Francisco, California, gave this metal tag to Owney. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Narrow horizontal plate has straight long edges and rounded ends.

items.title: Coat Room Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (3.81 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: The locations of some of the tags Owney received on his journeys are impossible to track down. This octagonal metal tag is marked simply “COATROOM 92” and offers no clues to its origin.
items.shapeEvidence: Clipped shoulders and angled lower corners create a many-sided outline.

items.title: Fordham Hotel Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 1/2 in. (5.08 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this brass tag from the Fordham Hotel in Paris, Kentucky. There is no available information to indicate when this tag was presented to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Angular upper shoulders narrow through curved sides to a bottom point.

items.title: San Francisco, California Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)

items.title: Chicago, Illinois Medallion Owney Tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 × 2 in. (5.08 × 5.08 cm)
items.description:
The dog that was called Owney by U.S. mail clerks had a 9-year career (1888-1897) as a self-appointed canine guardian of the mail and postal mascot. Beginning with his appearance in the fall of 1888 at the Albany, New York, Post Office, he accompanied mail pouches being forwarded by rail throughout the United States and the world.

When his railway excursions started, the Albany mail clerks began the tradition of the "Owney tag" by fastening a note to his collar asking employees of the Railway Mail Service to record his journeys by attaching leather and metal baggage tags. As this became popular, Postmaster General John Wanamaker presented the dog with a special harness-like jacket on which to distribute the tags. In addition to the 1893 Chicago, Illinois, Swedish medal shown here, Owney was presented with more than one thousand baggage claim tags, hotel key checks, tokens, badges, coins, buttons and other trinkets.

Owney's travels, recorded by these tags and legend, took him to Canada, Mexico and Alaska. And in 1895 he traveled from Tacoma, Washington to Japan, China, Singapore, Suez, Algiers and the Azores via the steamships "Victoria" and "Port Phillip" before returning to New York City and then by rail to Tacoma. He was sent by registered mail during part of this round-the-world journey, labeled as "Registered Dog Package".

Between 1893 and 1897, Owney was presented with many special awards and medals by kennel clubs and dog shows in recognition of his nationwide celebrity.

See also the related object records in this series ("Owney tags") and the record for the Dog: Owney.

Thousands of people, and at least one dog, visited the fair from across the US and around the world. The tag presented to Owney includes a representation of Christopher Columbus on one side and a list of names on the other: F.L. Block, V.B. Curtis, N.A. Mowr, F. Burdie, and J. Garsbard. One of Daniel Burham’s later projects was the City Post Office of Washington, DC, that is now home to the National Postal Museum.

items.description:
The dog that was called Owney by U.S. mail clerks had a 9-year career (1888-1897) as a self-appointed canine guardian of the mail and postal mascot. Beginning with his appearance in the fall of 1888 at the Albany, New York, Post Office, he accompanied mail pouches being forwarded by rail throughout the United States and the world.

When his railway excursions started, the Albany mail clerks began the tradition of the "Owney tag" by fastening a note to his collar asking employees of the Railway Mail Service to record his journeys by attaching leather and metal baggage tags. As this became popular, Postmaster General John Wanamaker presented the dog with a special harness-like jacket on which to distribute the tags. In addition to 1889 Exposition Universelle tag shown here, Owney was presented with more than one thousand baggage claim tags, hotel key checks, tokens, badges, medals, coins, buttons and other trinkets. The back of this tag is marked "Republique Francaise / N.J. Schloss & Co."

Owney's travels, recorded by these tags and legend, took him to Canada, Mexico and Alaska. And in 1895 he traveled from Tacoma, Washington to Japan, China, Singapore, Suez, Algiers and the Azores via the steamships "Victoria" and "Port Phillip" before returning to New York City and then by rail to Tacoma. He was sent by registered mail during part of this round-the-world journey, labeled as "Registered Dog Package".

Between 1893 and 1897, Owney was presented with many special awards and medals by kennel clubs and dog shows in recognition of his nationwide celebrity.

This is one of three tags that had been fastened together on Owney's jacket. The other two are 0.052985.219 and .220.
items.shapeEvidence: Main medallion is a round disk below the loop.

items.title: Worcester, Massachusetts Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag from a druggist in Worcester, Massachusetts. Phenyo Caffein Company produced a series of metal tangle puzzles dubbed the “Chilian [sic] Puzzle” and distributed as an advertising gimmick for their headache medicine. The token Owney received was only a small part of the original puzzle, which included another token of the same size, a ring, and chain with long links. The challenge in this puzzle was to untangle and free the ring on the device and then put it back on. The Phenyo Caffein Company was owned by Julius Garst and based in Worcester, Massachusetts. Garst, originally from Ohio, worked as a physician in Worcester through the 1890s.

items.description: One token Owney received while visiting St. Louis, Missouri was from a company that is still in existence today. This token came from an employee of the Anheuser-Busch Brewing Association. The token includes the company’s symbol on one side (the Eagle and letter A had been used to identify the company since 1872), and a notice celebrating annual shipments of 20,000 train car loads of Budweiser for the year. Although the company’s products were shipped as cargo, not through the US mail, those employed by the company to move the cargo undoubtedly interacted with other workers on the train cars, including the Railway Post Office clerks (and their occasional canine visitor). The company had begun using refrigerated railway cars in the 1880s.

Lincoln was a popular railway stop, serviced by a number of lines during Owney’s lifetime, including the Sioux City & Pacific; the Union Pacific; the Missouri Pacific; the Burlington & Missouri River; and the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific lines.

The medal face features the mythological three-headed dog Cerberus, who guarded the underworld. Such an image would be quite appropriate for Owney, who was famous as a guardian of mail bags. The back of the medal is engraved “Awarded to Owney the Globe Trotter, Chicago, 1897.”

items.title: S.C. Kennel Club Owney tag

items.description:
Owney received this specially engraved medal when he attended the Southern California Kennel Club in April 1893. According to a report in the Los Angeles Times on April 21, 1893, Owney was a star of the show. His presence was not only noted in a headline to the story “Owney, the Mail Service Traveler, on Exhibition,” but was the leading story in the newspaper’s report on the show. “Contrary to the general rules of bench shows, Owney, the celebrated canine traveler . . . was yesterday taken in charge by the club and assigned to a stall near the entrance, where he has been a drawing card all day.” The medallion reads:

Bench Show

S.C. Kennel Club

Los Angeles, Cal.

April 1893

Special for best Traveled dog.

items.description: Owney received this specially-engraved medal during an 1896 dog show in Grand Rapids, Michigan. The tag notes that it was awarded to “Owney the Globe Trotter” by the Butterfly Bench Show of Grand Rapids. On December 10, 1896, the Los Angeles Times noted that the show opened with “300 entries divided into eighty classes. The exhibits are of a much better class than last year, including some of the finest dogs in the country.” Owney’s fame as a “Globe Trotter” was in reference to the trip he made the previous fall, following mailbags around the world on ocean steamers.

items.title: Pacific Kennel Club Owney tag

items.description: Owney received this specially-engraved medal during his 1893 appearance at San Francisco’s Pacific Kennel Club dog show. A San Francisco Call reporter “interviewed” Owney for the paper, noting that the dog had “risen from comparative obscurity to be the best-known dog in the United States.” According to the reporter, Owney’s reply was a canine variation of the American “can do” spirit. That Owney “wishes it represents in the minds of the people that he is an example of what a dog can do for himself if he will only try.” The reverse of the medal is inscribed: "Presented to Owney by the Pacific Kennel Club / San Francisco / May 6, 1893."

items.description:
Owney received this celebration token while visiting Mitchell, South Dakota. The front of the token displays an image of the city’s 1892 Corn Belt Exposition building of 1892. The exposition, which ran from September 28 to October 6, 1892, helped lay the foundation for the creation of the “Mitchell Corn Palace” which remains a popular tourist attraction today. The back of the tag includes a short verse titled “South Dakota’s Invitation” and reads:

TO THE WEST OF MINNESOTA

AND BEYOND FAIR IOWA TOO,

LIES THE COUNTRY SOUTH DAKOTA,

WHERE THE SKIES ARE EVER BLUE.

SO STRANGER COME AND FIND A HOME

IF FORTUNE YOU PURSUE,

AND JUST THE PLACE FOR YOU.

items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)

Tumble of Corry, Pennsylvania, whose name is written on the inside of the tag, along with the number 93, indicating the year (1893) that Tumble presented this token to Owney.

This tag style was patented as noted on the tag on January 27, 1895. The patent was held by Frederick H. Laforge and J. Richard Smith of Watertown, Connecticut. Laforge and Smith were both officers in the Connecticut Mutual Steam Boiler Inspection and Insurance Company. In later years Smith manufactured metal novelties and Laforge continued work as a boiler inspector.

The back side of the token notes that it was: “good for one drink.” There is no additional information available to indicate when the token was given to the dog. Trade checks were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.

Paso Robles, located in San Luis Obispo County, California, was along a branch of the Atlantic and Pacific Railroad. The luxurious, three-story hotel opened in 1891. It included a beauty parlor, barber shop, library and billiard rooms. Guests could also enjoy the hotel’s large garden and golf course.
