items.title: Blanchester, Ohio Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
items.description: Owney received this trade check token from Wilson & Swing’s Billiard Hall in Blanchester, Ohio. The token was good for “5-cents at the bar.” There is no indication on the tag when it was given to the dog. Owney may have traveled to the town on the Baltimore & Ohio Southwest railroad, or the Cincinnati, Washington, and Baltimore Railroad.
items.shapeEvidence: Round token with a damaged top opening.

items.title: Camp Douglas, Wisconsin Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 3/16 x 1 1/8 in. (5.56 x 2.86 cm)
items.description: Owney received this dog license tag while visiting Camp Douglas, Wisconsin. Camp Douglas was a small, but busy town along the railways between Milwaukee, Wisconsin and Minneapolis/St. Paul, Minnesota and where east and west trains intersected with the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad. There is no information on who purchased the license for Owney, or when it was given to the dog.
items.shapeEvidence: Rounded upper shoulders taper to a pointed lower tip.

items.title: Bald Knob, Arkansas Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 × 15/16 in. (2.38 × 2.38 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification token from Lawrence J. Dumas of Bald Knob, Arkansas. Dumas had a small drug store in the city. Bald Knob was located on the St. Louis Iron Mountain & Southern railway line. There is no additional information on when Dumas gave this token to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular medal with a smooth rounded outer boundary.

items.title: Binghamton, New York Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/16 x 3/4 in. (3.33 x 1.91 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification token from Albert H. Surdam, a letter carrier from Binghamton, New York. The tag notes that Surdam lived on Rutherford Street in Binghamton, but there is no additional information to indicate when he presented the tag to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Wide horizontal elliptical plate.

items.title: Edward P. Thorn Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1/2 x 2 1/4 in. (1.27 x 5.72 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification token from Edward P. Thorn, a saloon keeper, wines and liquors dealer from Plainfield, New Jersey. Symbols on the token indicate Thorn was a Freemasons Lodge Master. Plainfield was a stop along the Central Railroad of New Jersey.
items.shapeEvidence: Horizontal elliptical engraved plate.

items.title: Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 × 1 3/16 in. (3.02 × 3.02 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token while traveling in the West. The name Sumas could indicate a hotel or business in the Dakota Territory, or the town of Sumas, Washington, along the Canadian border. There is no additional information to indicate exactly where Owney was when he received this token.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular main disk; the upper ring is excluded.

items.title: Los Angeles, California Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 7/16 × 1 7/16 in. (3.65 × 3.65 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification token from David L. Burke of Los Angeles, California. Burke owned a plumbing business. It is not known when or why he presented this token to the dog. Owney visited the city of Los Angeles several times, including once in 1893 when he was the star of a dog show in the city.
items.shapeEvidence: Round medal with fine, mostly uniform rim decoration.

items.title: Pontiac, Illinois Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 7/8 in. (4.45 x 2.22 cm)
items.description: Owney received this watch fob token from the Caldwell & McGregor jewelry store in Pontiac, Illinois. Although there is no information to indicate when the token was presented to the dog, James Caldwell retired and dissolved the partnership in 1895. Pontiac was easily reached by numerous railways, including the Wabash, the Chicago & Alton; and the Illinois Central railway lines.
items.shapeEvidence: Round-ended key-like body with a tapered stem and stepped opposite end.

items.title: Plymouth, New Hampshire Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 x 2 7/16 in. (1.59 x 6.19 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag from William G. Hull, who served as the postmaster of Plymouth, New Hampshire from 1895-1899. Prior to his service as postmaster of Plymouth, Hull had served as the first postmaster of Livingston, New Hampshire in 1881. Hull dated this tag as “M. 5. 96.” The town of Plymouth was reached by the Boston, Concord, Montreal & White Mountains railroad as well as the Pemigewasset Valley Railroad during Owney’s lifetime.
items.shapeEvidence: A narrow horizontal plate with long parallel straight edges and rounded short ends.

items.title: Madison, Wisconsin Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 × 1 in. (2.54 × 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification token from Charles G. Snow of Madison, Wisconsin. There is no information to indicate when Snow gave this token to the dog. Snow held several jobs. During the years Owney was traveling, Snow worked for the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad. From 1890-18 he was an assistant night clerk for the railroad. From 1894-1895, he was a freight clerk for the company.
items.shapeEvidence: Round disk; the enlarged hole remains internal.

items.title: Kansas City Post Office Department Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 5/8 in. (4.45 x 4.13 cm)
items.description:
Owney received this token from postal clerks in Kansas City, Missouri. The item is dated March 23, 1894, one of many trips Owney made through the area. This token was produced by the Henry J. Brunner’s Hardware Company of Kansas City. The company began as a repair shop and grew into a metal and machinist supply company.

Kansas City was a major railway hub and Owney would have traveled through the town on many occasions. Among the train lines that passed through during his lifetime were the Kansas City, Osceola, & Southern Railway; the Atchison, Topeka & the Santa Fe; the Chicago, Milwaukee, & St. Paul; and the Kansas City, Pittsburgh, & Gulf railroads.
items.shapeEvidence: The broad baggage plate has nearly straight sides and a rounded flat lower edge; the raised upper handle does not change its principally rectangular body.

items.title: Chicago, Illinois Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this advertising token from Dallemand & Co., a wholesale liquor supply company based in Chicago, Illinois. The company was operated by Albert Dallemand. There is no indication from the token when it was given to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Near-round silver medal body.

items.title: Taunton Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 13/16 x 1 13/16 in. (2.06 x 4.6 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag from members of the Taunton, Massachusetts post office. The Taunton post office provided their own, phonetic, spelling of Owney’s name, engraving the tag to “Onee” and presenting it to the dog on June 9, 1894. Taunton was an active railroad town, with a number of lines passing through.
items.shapeEvidence: A horizontal plate with parallel straight long edges, short straight ends and rounded corners.

items.title: W.C. Munsey & Co. Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this trade check token during his travels. The token indicates that it is good for 10-cents off at “W.C. Munsey & Co.” on one side, and includes the name “Palace” and “Barber Shop & Bath House” on the other. San Francisco, California had a large and famous hotel known as the “Palace,” but at this time there is no known connection between that hotel and “W.C. Munsey & Co.”
items.shapeEvidence: Circular medal body; the projecting clip is excluded.

items.title: Cheyenne, Wyoming Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1/2 × 1/2 in. (1.27 × 1.27 cm)
items.description: Owney received this medal from the postal workers of the Cheyenne, Wyoming post office on April 12, 1893. At that time, that office had a postmaster, three clerks, and six city letter carriers. The reverse side of the medal advertises the city of “Fair” Gallatin, Montana, nicknamed the “Egypt of America” by promoters for its fertile and productive soil. The medal may have been handy when Owney was visiting Cheyenne’s postal workers, who scratched and engraved their message into one side of the medal. The city of Gallatin is just over Wyoming’s northern border, while Cheyenne is in the far south-eastern corner.
items.shapeEvidence: A circular coin body with an internal hole near the upper edge.

items.title: San Francisco, California Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 x 7/8 in. (5.4 x 2.22 cm)
items.description: Owney received this advertising and identification token from the Home Benefit Life Association of San Francisco, California. The token includes the embossed image of a building on one side and the “reward return to” identification on the other. There is nothing on the tag to indicate when it was given to Owney. The association was established by Frank Colton in the early 1880s and went out of business in 1892. Owney made several trips to San Francisco during his lifetime.
items.shapeEvidence: Oval engraved main plate; its projecting suspension handle and ring are excluded.

items.title: Mitchell Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 x 15 3/16 in. (2.38 x 38.52 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token while visiting the town of Mitchell, South Dakota. As the tag notes, in 1889, Mitchell was still part of the Dakota Territory (the territory became North and South Dakota late in the year, on November 2, 1889). The Maltese-Cross-shaped tag includes the number 228. There is no additional information to indicate the purpose of the token.
items.shapeEvidence: Four flared arms make a cross-shaped body.

items.title: Waverly, Iowa Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/16 x 1 5/16 in. (2.7 x 3.33 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification token from Grant E. Hirleman in Waverly, Iowa. There is no additional information on the tag to indicate Hirleman’s connection to Owney or when he presented the token to the dog. Hirleman was not a postal employee in Iowa during the 1890s.
items.shapeEvidence: Ornate asymmetric scroll-shaped body with lobed ends.

items.title: Bloomington Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
items.description: Owney received this item during his travels. The lettering is badly faded, with little more than the individual’s first name “James” and the town of “Bloomington” [Indiana] still visible. There is no additional information on the full identity of the donor. The item was most likely a Civil War-era soldier’s identification tag. Such tags were purchased by soldiers who wanted to insure their bodies could be identified in case of death. There is nothing with this item to indicate when it was given to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Round worn metal disk with a continuous curved perimeter.

items.title: St. Louis, Missouri Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 × 1 3/16 in. (3.02 × 3.02 cm)
items.description: Owney received this advertising and personal identification token during his travels. The token was produced by the Cod-Liver Oil Glycerin Company of St. Louis, Missouri. The token advertised a new method of delivering cod liver as a medicine. The “Aluminum Pocket Piece” as it is identified on the back of the token, was given to physicians to advertise the new product. A space on the back of the token was left open for physicians to place their name and address. There is no information to indicate who gave the token to Owney or when it was given to the dog.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular disk with an internal side opening.

items.title: Portland, Oregon Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token from a group of Railway Mail Service (RMS) clerks working out of Portland, Oregon on a “South Bound” railway mail car. The token was originally produced by Mitchell Lewis & Staver Co., a Pacific Northwest machinery company that began in 1882 and is still in operation. The RMS clerks scratched out one face of the token and crudely engraved their identification information as well as the date, April 16, 1893, over that side of the coin.
items.shapeEvidence: A round medal disc with a continuous outer rim and an internal suspension hole.

items.title: St. Peter, Minnesota Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/16 × 1 5/16 in. (3.33 × 3.33 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification token from W.F. Coffin of St. Peter, Minnesota. The individual who presented this tag to Owney may have been Wilbur F. Coffin, a postal clerk. The token was probably created on the engraved date of 1880, at least eight years before Owney began making his journeys. It is not known when Owney was in St. Peter, but he probably arrived in town on the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad.
items.shapeEvidence: Ornate scroll-shaped plate with an asymmetrical lobed end.

items.title: Lawrence House Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 1/2 in. (4.45 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel room key token from the Lawrence House in Jackson, Mississippi. There is no additional information to indicate when the token was presented to the dog. Owney may have arrived in Jackson aboard the Illinois Central or the Yazoo & Mississippi Valley railroad.
items.shapeEvidence: Tall rectangular hotel plate with rounded corners.

items.title: Ranier Hotel Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 x 1 9/16 in. (2.38 x 3.97 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel room key token from the Rainier Hotel in Seattle, Washington. Owney made several visits to Seattle and its nearby neighbor Tacoma, Washington during his lifetime. The hotel was located between 5th and 6th avenues and between Marion and Columbia streets.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad angular shoulders taper to a pointed lower edge.

items.title: Pennsylvania and Erie Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 x 1 1/2 in. (2.38 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this railway baggage check token while traveling on the Pennsylvania and Erie Railroad. There is no additional information to indicate when the token was presented to the dog. The token was made by the Hoole Manufacturing Company of New York, owned and operated by Edmund Hoole.
items.shapeEvidence: Wide rectangular plate with rounded corners.

items.title: Plumb House Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 1 1/2 in. (4.13 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this hotel room key token from the Plumb House hotel in Streator, Illinois. There is no additional information on when the token was given to the dog. Plumb House, located on the northwest corner of Main and Bloomington, was named for Ralph Plumb, the town’s first mayor (1882-1885). In its early days, Streator was a coal town, and grew quickly as railway lines were built to carry out the coal. Several railway lines ran through the town during Owney’s lifetime, including the Chicago, Burlington, & Quincy; the Louisville, Evansville, & St. Louis Consolidated; the Chicago & Alton; and the Peoria, Decatur, & Evansville lines.
items.shapeEvidence: Multiple curved bulges and a lobed base create an ornamental outline.

items.title: Houston, Texas Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 7/8 × 7/8 in. (2.22 × 2.22 cm)
items.description: This is one of two tokens Owney received from Alphonse Stude’s Houston, Texas, bakery. Stude, a prominent Houston businessman and city booster, recognized the advertising potential of the traveling dog. Owney’s visits were often written up in local newspapers, with reporters often listing the tokens the dog was wearing at the time. This token, which could be used in trade for a small loaf of bread, is known as a trade check. Such tokens were used much like coupons are today, offered by merchants as a lure to increase customers’ purchases.
items.shapeEvidence: Eight straight sides form an octagonal token.

items.title: Chicago, Santa Fe, and California Railroad Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 × 1 3/16 in. (3.02 × 3.02 cm)
items.description: Owney received this railway bag check token while traveling on a local line of the Chicago, Santa Fe, and California Railroad. There is no additional information to indicate when or where the token was given to the dog. Like several other tokens presented to the dog, it was created by William W. Wilcox’s manufacturing company of Chicago, Illinois.
items.shapeEvidence: Wide plate with rounded rectangular perimeter.

items.title: Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 x 1 1/8 in. (2.86 x 2.86 cm)
items.description: Owney received this tag during his travels. One side of the tag includes the notation “1H” and the date “1893.” The other side has faintly legible scratches of names, “Jas Stone” and “Guy D. May” or “Guy D. Way.” There is no additional information to indicate the men’s connection to Owney or the post office.
items.shapeEvidence: Eight angular sides form a strongly cut-corner octagon.

items.title: Cincinnati Post Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 3/4 x 1 3/8 in. (1.91 x 3.49 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token while visiting Cincinnati, Ohio. The item may have been given to the dog by a representative of the ‘Cincinnati Post’ newspaper. There are no additional notations on the token to indicate its original function or when it was given to the dog. Owney could have arrived in town on a number of different railroads. Cincinnati grew from a bustling port city along the Ohio River into an active railroad town, with at least seven different rail lines leading into the city.
items.shapeEvidence: Four-sided rectangular plate with nearly square corners.

items.title: Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width x Depth: 1 x 1 1/2 x 1/2 in. (2.54 x 3.81 x 1.27 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token during his travels. The only information available on the item are the initials “N.U.H.” and the number 9. There is nothing to indicate when or where the token originated or who gave it to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Rectangular plate with a folded top edge and rounded lower corners.

items.title: San Antonio, Texas Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (3.81 × 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token from members of his greatest fan club--Railway Mail Service workers. These clerks worked out of the San Antonio, Texas post office. The token is dated April 4, 1892. Owney is known to have visited San Antonio at least twice, in 1892 and in 1895.
items.shapeEvidence: The main metal disc has a continuous round perimeter; the two suspension holes do not change its body shape.

items.title: Rock Island, Illinois Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/16 × 1 3/16 in. (3.02 × 3.02 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification token from John Koch, a Rock Island, Illinois gunsmith. The token includes Koch’s occupation on one side, along with the date May 9, 1895. Among the trains that Owney may have ridden on into the city were the Chicago, Rock Island, & Pacific; the Chicago & Alton; and the Chicago, Burlington, & Quincy railroads.
items.shapeEvidence: A circular body with a wide internal suspension slot near the upper edge.

items.title: Sanborn, Iowa Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1/2 × 1 1/2 in. (1.27 × 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token from Chauncey F. Owen, the postmaster of Sanborn, Iowa. Owen served as the town’s postmaster twice, from December 1884 to July 1885 and from February 1890 to January 1896. It would have been during his second term as Sanborn’s postmaster that he presented this token to Owney. During Owney’s lifetime, Sanborn was serviced by the Chicago, Milwaukee, & St. Paul railroad line.
items.shapeEvidence: Long rectangular nameplate with rounded ends and straight upper/lower edges.

items.title: Mitchell, South Dakota Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/4 × 1 1/4 in. (3.18 × 3.18 cm)
items.description: Owney received this dog license tag during a visit to Mitchell, South Dakota. The tag shows that someone has covered Owney’s dog tax, giving him legal permission to be on the city streets, at least during the year of 1890. The tag was manufactured by S.D. Childs & Company, a Chicago, Illinois stationery and engraving firm.
items.shapeEvidence: Angular many-sided numbered token.

items.title: Cedar Rapids, Iowa Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 5/8 x 1 1/4 in. (1.59 x 3.18 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token from someone in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The token has the phrase, “Love, Purity, Fidelity” on one side, which indicates it came from someone who was a member of the Freemasons. There is no additional information on the token to indicate when it was given to the dog and at the time, no postal workers from the Cedar Rapids post office were named Horace.
items.shapeEvidence: Horizontal elliptical engraved plate.

items.title: P.J. Butler Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 15/16 × 15/16 in. (2.38 × 2.38 cm)
items.description: Owney received this trade check token from P.J. Butler, possibly of Indianapolis, Indiana, but no additional information is available on the token to make certain identification. There is no information on the token to indicate when it was given to the dog.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular trade-token body.

items.title: Sioux City Corn Palace Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 15/16 in. (4.13 x 2.38 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token advertising the Corn Palace in Sioux City, Iowa. This was the last of corn palaces built in that city from 1887-1891. The 1891 Corn Palace featured a 200-foot tower with a balcony. There is no information indicating who presented this token to Owney.
items.shapeEvidence: Circular silver medal with a consistently rounded outer edge.

items.title: Pierre, South Dakota Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 15/16 in. (4.13 x 2.38 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token from the employees of the Pierre, South Dakota post office. At the time of Owney’s travels there were only three people employed at that post office. Robert N. Locke was the town’s postmaster and John H. McCord, originally of Illinois, and Fred S. Williams, born in Canada, served as the town’s postal clerks.
items.shapeEvidence: The elongated main body has straight sides, angled shoulders and noticeably clipped lower corners; the circular top lug is excluded.

items.title: Lawrence, Massachusetts Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/8 x 1 1/2 in. (5.4 x 3.81 cm)
items.description: Owney received this advertising token from George Ketchum, a pharmacist who partnered with H.M. Witney in Lawrence, Massachusetts. The store was named for Whitney and located on 297 Essex Street. Ketchum had the token engraved especially for the dog, “Presented to Owney” and included the presentation date of April 25, 1896 at the bottom of the token.
items.shapeEvidence: A tall narrow oval with smoothly curved sides and rounded upper and lower ends.

items.title: Jackson, Mississippi Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/8 × 1 1/8 in. (2.86 × 2.86 cm)
items.description: Owney received this identification token from W. M. Bettersworth of Jackson, Mississippi. The token is dated1895. The token’s design shows that Bettersworth was a member of the Knights of Pythius, the “FCB” in the design standing for “friendship, charity, and benevolence.” There is no information with the token to indicate Bettersworth relationship with the Post Office Department, if any.
items.shapeEvidence: Round medal with a fine regular serrated rim.

items.title: Hillsboro, Ohio Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 in. (3.81 x 2.54 cm)
items.description: Owney received this advertising token in the shape of a pocket watch from F. Emmerling, a jeweler living in Hillsboro, Ohio. There is no information on when Emmerling gave the token to the dog. The back side carries the advertisements for “Jas. Boss” “Keystone Watch Cases.” Watch cases were sold separately from the pocket watch. Boss Keystone cases were among the most popular watch cases. The advertisement notes that Emmerling carried this cases, including the new “non-pull-out-bow” a fastener that had been patented by Keystone Watch Case Company employee Edward Chappatte in 1891.
items.shapeEvidence: Vertically oval watch-case-shaped body below a separate bow.

items.title: Bozeman, Montana Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 1/2 x 1 1/8 in. (3.81 x 2.86 cm)
items.description: Owney received this dog license tag while visiting Bozeman, Montana in 1892. There is no additional information to indicate who presented it to the dog. The tag was manufactured by E.R. Williamson of Minneapolis, Minnesota.
items.shapeEvidence: Broad rounded shoulders taper to a small pointed bottom.

items.title: Omaha & OGD Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 1 9/16 in. (4.13 x 3.97 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token while traveling on board the Omaha & Ogden railway mail route. The token is dated April 22, but no year is indicated. The token was given to Owney by the clerks working on the eastbound train car, Michael P. Burke, an Irish immigrant, Joseph F. Finch of Illinois, Lawrence J.A. Holst, a German immigrant, Warren J. Nash of Maine, Lawrence R. Rossiter of Ohio, Frederick R. Stuart and George G. Whitmore, both born in Nebraska.
items.shapeEvidence: Angular upper shoulders and indented sides lead to a pointed lower edge.

items.title: Grand Rapids, Michigan Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 x 1 1/4 in. (5.72 x 3.18 cm)
items.description: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. The plate was given to the dog while he was visiting Grand Rapids, Michigan in September 1896. It notes that for Owney, at least, there was such a thing as a “free lunch,” at least in Grand Rapids. That year Owney also received a specially-engraved medal from the Butterfly Bench Show of Grand Rapids (object number 0.52985.336).
items.shapeEvidence: Featured plaque has straight upper/lower edges and a rounded right end; mounting is omitted in this detail.

items.title: Milwaukee, Wisconsin Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 x 1 1/4 in. (5.08 x 3.18 cm)
items.description: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. He received it while in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on February 27, 1896. While the tag encourages Owney to “call again,” there is no additional information to indicate who attached this tag to the dog’s collar. Several railway lines ran through Milwaukee, connecting it with Chicago to the south and Minneapolis to the west, including the Chicago, Milwaukee, & St. Paul Railroad.
items.shapeEvidence: A rectangular collar plate with straight horizontal upper and lower edges and straight short sides.

items.title: Rock Island, Illinois Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 5/8 x 1 3/16 in. (6.67 x 3.02 cm)
items.description: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. He received it from the Rock Island, Illinois railway postal clerks while visiting the city in 1895.
items.shapeEvidence: Featured plaque is rectangular with modest clipped corners.

items.title: Albany, New York Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 7/8 x 1 1/4 in. (7.3 x 3.18 cm)
items.description: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. The scalloped-edged plate bearing his name was attached to his collar by the workers at the Albany, New York post office. Owney began his travels from Albany and that city’s postal workers considered him to be part of their postal family. There is no information to indicate when this plate was attached to Owney’s collar.
items.shapeEvidence: Main plaque is rectangular, with a small regular scalloped border.

items.title: Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 2 1/4 x 1 in. (5.72 x 2.54 cm)
items.description: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. He received it while visiting Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania in 1892. The tag includes the number “166.” There is no definitive information available at this time to indicate the purpose of the tag, or who gave it to the dog. Numerous railway lines passed through Pittsburgh during Owney’s lifetime.
items.shapeEvidence: Wide featured plaque with straight opposing edges.

items.title: Bay City, Michigan Fire Department Owney tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 5/8 x 1 1/4 in. (4.13 x 3.18 cm)
items.description: This is one of six metal plates attached to Owney’s collar. It was placed on his collar by members of the Bay City, Michigan Fire Department during an 1896 visit. A number of railroad lines traveled through Bay City, including the Grand Rapids & Indiana; Wabash; Chicago & Western Michigan; Michigan Central; and Manistee & Northeastern railroads.
items.shapeEvidence: Featured plaque is broadly rectangular with slightly shaped upper corners.

items.title: Louisville, Kentucky Owney Tag
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 5 1/2 x 1 1/2 in. (13.97 x 3.81 cm)
items.shapeEvidence: Long crescent-like curved tag tapers toward one end.

items.title: Canadian Owney tag
places: British Columbia & Vancouver Island (British colony; Canadian pr
items.dimensions: Height x Width: 1 3/4 x 1 5/8 in. (4.45 x 4.13 cm)
items.description: Owney received this token from “E.O. Atkinson” and “A.N. Trew” on July 1, 1895. The token notes two locations, Calgary, Alberta, and Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. Owney made at least one trip to Vancouver, Canada, during his lifetime.
items.shapeEvidence: A broad upper plate narrows through curved lower sides into a central bottom point.
